One percent is not a policy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Almost every recent graduate with physical disability has a similar story to share about finding work. The certificate on the wall is not as valuable as it should be, and years of applications and exams come to an end when they lose their position for disabilities.
The number tells the same story more bluntly. Fewer than one in five people with disabilities in Bangladesh are currently in any kind of work . Not fewer than one in five disabled graduates, specifically one in five of the entire working-age disabled population, degree or no degree. For a country that spent a decade insisting a diploma is the ticket out of poverty, that statistic is an indictment.
The state has not been silent on this. It has simply been vague, and vagueness has done the work of exclusion just as effectively as outright refusal would have.
In 2012, the Bangladesh Public Service Commission introduced a 1% quota for disabled candidates in civil service recruitment. Long before that, the government had already declared a supposedly generous 10% job quota covering both people with disabilities and orphans together , without ever specifying how that 10% should be divided between the two groups, a decision so poorly designed that disability advocates have called it effectively meaningless as an employment right.
When the 2024 quota reform movement forced the Supreme Court to redraw the entire system, the final settlement allotted just 1% of civil service posts jointly to disabled people and the third gender combined , applied only at the interview stage after every applicant has already cleared the same written examinations everyone else must pass. That is not affirmative action. It is a rounding error dressed up as policy.
This is the quieter sequel to a movement most of the world already knows the ending of. The student protesters who brought down a government in 2024 were demanding a merit-based system, and they got one: 93% of government jobs are now allocated by merit alone.
It was, on its own terms, a democratic victory. But merit-based recruitment only works as a fair system if everyone arrives at the starting line with a genuinely equal shot, and disabled candidates in Bangladesh do not.
They arrive after a school system that pushed most of them out before secondary level, after a university system that could not accommodate their degree of choice, and after years of accumulated disadvantage that a written exam does nothing to correct.
Reducing the disability quota to a rounding error, in the same reform that celebrated merit, quietly assumed away everything that made the playing field unequal in the first place.
Ahead of this year's national election, that contradiction did not go unnoticed. Disability Rights Watch and Transparency International Bangladesh publicly pressed political parties to commit to a 2% quota for persons with disabilities in government jobs , along with guaranteed representation in parliament and reserved seats in local government.
Their argument was not radical. It was an appeal to enforce rights the country had already promised on paper. Bangladesh ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities back in 2007, passed its own Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act in 2013, and adopted a National Action Plan in 2019.
Nearly two decades of legal commitments, and the advocacy groups making that appeal still had to explain, in a press conference, that enforcement has remained thin and that disabled citizens continue to face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment as a matter of routine.
The private sector offers little refuge from this pattern. There is no meaningful quota requirement for private employers at all, which means the vast majority of Bangladesh's job market, the banks, the garment industry, the booming fintech and e-commerce startups that dominate headlines about the country's economic future operates under no obligation to hire disabled graduates whatsoever.
Those who do find private-sector work often describe being underpaid, given no real accommodation, and offered little legal recourse if they are pushed out. A country can build all the accessible universities in the world and it will not matter if the market at the other end of that pipeline treats a disabled degree-holder as a liability rather than an asset.
None of this requires Bangladesh to invent a new policy framework from scratch. It requires enforcing the one that already exists and being honest about its inadequacy.
Raise the joint 1% quota to a level that actually reflects the size of the disabled population it claims to represent, and disaggregate it so third-gender and disabled applicants are no longer competing against each other for the same sliver of opportunity.
Extend meaningful, monitored hiring obligations into the private sector, not as a symbolic gesture but with real reporting requirements and real penalties for non-compliance.
And stop treating disability employment as a separate, lesser conversation from the broader push for a merit-based, accountable state that the last two years of protest were supposedly about.
The graduates who sat outside Dhaka University's Raju Memorial Sculpture last October were not asking Bangladesh to lower its standards for them. They were asking it to notice that the standards it already has were never built with them in mind.
A country that just rewrote its rules for who gets hired into government service has no excuse left for pretending that question is too complicated to answer.
Farhana Kabir is a social science researcher focusing on inequality, education, and policy in Bangladesh.

item.title: PCB appoints South Africa's Michael Smith as batting coach for Pakistan men's cricket team. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Former South African cricketer Michael Smith has been appointed as the batting coach of the Pakistan men’s cricket team for two years, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) announced on Tuesday.

According to a press release issued by the PCB, the “46-year-old will work with the team across both red-ball and white-ball formats”.

He will join the Pakistan team ahead of the three-match Test series against England, commencing on Aug 19, the press release stated.

Elaborating on Smith’s experience, the press release stated that he had featured in 89 first-class matches, 72 List-A matches and 16 T20 matches between 2003 and 2013.

“The right-handed batter scored 7,029 runs across the three formats, including nine centuries and 40 half-centuries,” the PCB said.

Smith, who holds a Level 4 coaching qualification, has served on the coaching staffs of three HBL Pakistan Super League (PSL) franchises — Islamabad United, Karachi Kings and Multan Sultans, it added

The press release further stated that he has also worked as a batting coach with Australian franchise Hobart Hurricanes and Cricket Tasmani.

As a coaching consultant, Smith has worked with South Africa’s KZN Inland and Eastern Province, the press release added.

Prior to Smith’s appointment, former Test batter Asad Shafiq was appointed as Pakistan’s interim batting coach in April 2026 for the Bangladesh Test series. Shafiq is currently also accompanying the Pakistan team for its two-match Test series in the West Indies.

Before Shafiq’s interim appointment, Shahid Aslam had been serving as Pakistan’s batting coach since replacing former Test captain Mohammad Yousuf in the role in November 2024.

The decline of academic integrity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is troubling and, frankly, embarrassing to see recent findings by the Prothom Alo that identified serious inconsistencies in research papers published by respected journals and involving authors from renowned academic institutions of the country.
That such irregularities could make their way into publications associated with prestigious institutions is nothing short of shameful. Regardless of whether these issues stem from deliberate misconduct or failures in oversight, they expose weaknesses in a system that is expected to uphold the highest standards of academic integrity -- which is the foundation upon which research, innovation, and public trust are built.
When that foundation is compromised through dishonest practices, therefore, the damage extends far beyond individual careers; it undermines the credibility of institutions, weakens confidence in scholarly work, and tarnishes a country's academic standing.
It goes without saying that the loss of credibility through dishonest measures is simply unacceptable under any circumstances. It is even more alarming at a time when Bangladesh is already battling a dwindling confidence in its educational and academic honour.
Our universities and researchers deserve recognition for genuine contributions, not suspicion generated by the actions of a few. However, every case of questionable research makes it harder for honest academics to earn the trust and respect they deserve on the global stage.
This is precisely why institutions must treat research integrity as a non-negotiable priority. Stronger screening mechanisms, rigorous peer review, mandatory ethics training, and meaningful accountability for misconduct are essential.
Furthermore, publishers, universities, and regulatory bodies all have a responsibility to ensure that fraudulent or manipulated research has no place in academic literature.
Bangladesh has no shortage of talented scholars capable of producing world-class research. Protecting their reputation requires an uncompromising commitment to honesty and transparency.
Academic prestige cannot be manufactured through shortcuts; it can only be earned through credible, ethical, and verifiable scholarship -- and that is the standard our institutions must uphold.

item.title: Creating an inclusive nation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The findings of the recent election observation report, which highlighted the significant barriers faced by millions of voters with disabilities, are deeply concerning.
While Bangladesh has made progress in strengthening its electoral institutions, these shortcomings demonstrate that inclusivity remains an unfinished task.
The right to vote is not a privilege reserved for those without physical or sensory limitations; it is a fundamental constitutional right that must be guaranteed to every citizen.
When polling centres are inaccessible, election materials are unavailable in appropriate formats, or adequate assistance is lacking, citizens with disabilities are effectively excluded from participating in decisions that shape the nation's future.
Such barriers undermine not only individual rights but also the legitimacy of the democratic process itself.
Addressing these issues does not require extraordinary measures; it requires sustained commitment. Ensuring polling stations are physically accessible, election officials receive proper disability-awareness training, and voting materials are available in formats suitable for people with visual, hearing, or other impairments should be the bare minimum.
For that, collaboration with disability rights organizations can help identify practical solutions rather than treating accessibility as an afterthought.
An inclusive electoral system also sends a broader message about society's values. When citizens see that every individual, regardless of ability, is respected and empowered to participate, the public's collective confidence in democratic institutions grows.
Conversely, leaving millions to navigate preventable obstacles signals that some voices matter less than others.
A democracy can only be considered truly representative when every eligible citizen is able to exercise the right to vote with dignity, independence, and equal access, and Bangladesh has repeatedly expressed its commitment to this very cause.
These commitments must, therefore, be reflected where they matter most: In protecting citizens' fundamental rights.
It is our democratic imperative to ensure that every citizen can cast a ballot -- as well as exercise their other fundamental rights -- safely, independently, and without discrimination.

item.title: Invest in the real talent. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The FIFA World Cup 2026 left a sobering message: -- the euphoria surrounding football and stardom was overshadowed by parochial nationalism, hostile fan culture, and highly controversial decisions. Exorbitant broadcasting fees and ticket prices exposed the organizers' blatant commercial greed.
So, the largest sporting event in the world no longer offers recreation; neither does it promote the so-called sporting spirit among the teams and fans. Was forcing the Iranian team to leave American soil immediately after each match truly a gesture of “promoting friendship through football?”
Captivating nations and up to two billion spectators sprawling all over the world, the football extravaganza has stopped even intelligent people from asking how sponsors spending billions of dollars would recover the money.
Will the burden not be shifted to those who bought whatever needed to watch the matches and spent sleepless nights?
Whether they are conscious of it or not, they are the consumers of football fever and also of the expensive products and services of the sponsor companies.
The WC football hype was unparalleled in Bangladesh, perhaps more “madness” than in famous footballing nations like Argentina and Brazil. While we don't dare to dream of playing in the finals, Bangladesh recorded the highest number of fan fatalities -- at least 11 out of 20 or so deaths.
The stories of the footballing event and players and coaches, be it the most insignificant ones, flooded the valuable spaces of the media, especially the homepages online. Such coverage was not compatible with the practice in the media of most participating nations, let alone elsewhere.
Isn't it the poverty of the media as well because rather than asking questions about propriety, they competed with each other to capture public attention? Bangladesh had more serious issues to deal with. Yet, we wasted our working hours for over 40 days, doing “research,” forecasting, and gossiping about this tournament.
Brazil's 1994 WC winning footballer Romario once said money for stadiums should instead go toward essential public needs like health, education, and social welfare. Perhaps we should take note.
Currently, Bangladesh's football ranking among 211 nations is 181st. There is no reason why we should feel ashamed of it. Every nation will not shine in every area and Bangladesh, too, is not expected to chase every goal in all global events.
However, there is nothing wrong in targeting to attain success in sports and athletics where there is realistic potential.
The government has just completed a program styled “Notun Kuri Sports” for discovering young sporting talents. This has been organized in the light of Bangladesh Television's Notun Kuri, a program to hunt young talents of the entertainment arena.
Focusing on finding any talent is not only encouraging for the young minds who want to grow, but also a good investment for the future of the nation. In our context, achieving success in sports and entertainment is widely believed to be an easy formula for life, which is not the case in reality.
However, if we are to prosper, making scientific progress, creating knowledge of arts, excelling in creative works, innovation in technology, attaining higher capacity in engineering and medical sciences, offering unique business ideas, acquiring better skills in various trades and services, and moral leadership and social development and harmony and all such areas are better suited.
We are yet to see talent hunt programs in disciplines where the country seriously lags behind the developed nations. We may have plenty of natural but unflourished talents that are not being recognized.
Bangladesh needs all those promising youth who, too, need support from the state to become what they dream of and give back to society. It is time to realize the aspirations of the 2024 revolution, spearheaded by the younger generations.
Khawaza Main Uddin is a journalist. He can be contacted at khawaza@gmail.com .

item.title: Ownership, arrogance, and the spirit of July. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A video has gone viral in the last 48 hours from Uttarkhan, Dhaka, on the night of August 2, 2026. The administrator and his companion, introduced as a local government official, confront an aged person in grey hair in front of a garment factory. The gentleman, on their insistence, identifies as a partner of the factory and introduces himself as Col Zakir.
The two gentlemen charged Col Zakir as to why he had beaten their people. He politely asks if it seemed that he could beat up people. Colonel Zakir is seen to have remained composed in spite of all the shouting and instigation and replying in a low tone.
In response, the two gentlemen who introduced themselves as government officials shout back: "Do you know who I am? You haven't become such a big thing that you can do whatever you want. Did you think you founded the Awami League?"
Moments later, according to eyewitnesses, police detained the colonel and 22 workers and kept them in lockup without an FIR.
Does the administrator have any magisterial power to order arrest of an individual? What happened in Uttarkhan is a textbook violation of the rule of law.
Now let us see who can issue arrests. Under CrPC Section 54, 55, 59 and 151, only: A police officer on his own assessment of cognizable offense, or a magistrate under Section 44, or on a written order/warrant under Section 75.
Since a DNCC Administrator is not a magistrate and is appointed under Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009, Section 25A (as amended for interim government) as an administrative head to run routine functions, he has no power. Only the DC can empower someone as executive magistrate, and to that a gazette notification is required. So his shouting: " Arrest hobe, maamla hobe " -- is legally void. It is intimidation, not an order.
The next question is whether the police could arrest on his shouting. No. Under Section 149, 150 CrPC and Police Regulations of Bengal (PRB) Regulation 120, the police must exercise independent judgment. If police shoved and detained Col Zakir because the administrator said so, that is illegal detention under Section 342 of Penal Code and violation of Article 33 of the Constitution.
What should have happened?
If there was a dispute, the administrator could call the concerned executive magistrate or the OC of Uttarkhan police station to intervene. Police should have separated both parties, taken them to the police station, recorded a GD, and allowed both to file complaints. Detention beyond 24 hours without producing before a magistrate under Article 33(2) and CrPC 61 is illegal.
May we humbly request the administrator and the honorable MP to consider whether such behavior is congenial to the rule of law?
This is the sort of behaviour that July 2024 was against. This is "might is right" replacing "rule of law," When an unelected administrator behaves like a colonial magistrate, and police act like his private force, it contradicts Article 27 which states that all citizens are equal before law.
If a retired officer of the Bangladesh Army, who served the state, can be shoved aside on a political shout, what protection does a common garment worker have?
This is the culture we need to come out of. If government officials and employees had taken true ownership of their duties with efficiency, honesty, and patriotism, politicians would never dare to behave like this.
The truth is bitter: A large section of our political class lacks patriotism, honesty, proper education, and a sense of justice and equity.
This vacuum is exploited by a section of dishonest bureaucrats who collude with these politicians for unethical gains. And at the end of the day, the same politicians humiliate the very civil servants they corrupted.
We created this opportunity for them. The historic chance for nation-building was wasted. The profound sacrifice of July 2024 created the chance to reset the state which we are squandering.
The pledge of July -- to establish the rule of law - is being grossly ignored. The sacrifice of thousands of martyrs and the maimed is being betrayed.
A nation rises on patriotism, visionary leadership, and wisdom. But due to political disunity, short-sightedness, lack of patriotism, and dishonesty, for 55 years, we have been destroying our own country.
We do not learn from history. Just two years ago, we saw how students and the masses did not even give Sheikh Hasina time to finish her cooked lunch. She had to eat it in Delhi. Power is temporary. Arrogance is fatal.
Therefore, to implement the aspirations of July, all political parties must unite and exercise restraint. Government employees must take ownership of the country, and dishonest politicians cannot turn it again into a haven of corruption and plunder.
Otherwise, the fire smoldering under the ashes may flare up again. The common people will return to demand what they have wanted for 55 years: The rule of law.
Let this video be a wake-up call. If a retired colonel who gave his youth to the country is not safe from public humiliation, no ordinary citizen is safe anywhere.
Brig Gen Qazi Abidus Samad, ndc, psc (Retd) is a freelance contributor.

item.description:
For 115 days, captain Mohammad Shafiqul Islam was stranded on the high seas of the Gulf, watching missiles light up the night sky and rationing food and water for his crew.

"I tried to stay calm because I was responsible for 31 lives, a ship worth $40 million, and cargo valued at $8.2 million," the 51-year-old Bangladeshi mariner told AFP, back home after the ordeal.

Islam was the captain of the Banglar Joyjatra, a bulk carrier that had arrived in the Gulf a month before the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February.
